summary: This document updates the TLS Transport Model for SNMP (RFC 6353) so it works with TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3. It remains compatible with TLS and DTLS 1.2. It also updates the SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB defined in RFC 6353.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret-message lock for network gadgets got a newer, better version. This document updates the old SNMP lock instructions so they work with the new lock.

questions: what is the snmp-tlstm hashalgorithms registry
what does rfc 9456 change in rfc 6353
subtitle: Brings SNMP over TLS up to date for TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3, with a new hash registry and a ban on 0-RTT.

tldr.problem: RFC 6353 defined how SNMP runs over TLS and DTLS, but some of its rules, such as the fingerprint hash identifier and session resumption, did not fit TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9456 moves the one-octet hash identifier to a new IANA 'SNMP-TLSTM HashAlgorithms' registry, requires (D)TLS 1.2 or later, forbids 0-RTT, and republishes the SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB with clarified wording.
tldr.outcome: SNMP over (D)TLS can use TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3 while staying compatible with (D)TLS 1.2. The RFC updates RFC 6353.

today: RFC 9456 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023. It updates RFC 6353 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why RFC 6353 Needed an Update
sections.content:
The TLS Transport Model (TLSTM) lets SNMP messages travel inside a TLS or DTLS connection. This document updates and clarifies how the rules of RFC 6353 apply when TLS or DTLS versions later than 1.2 are used. It calls the two protocols together "(D)TLS". It also stresses the requirement in RFC 8996 that prohibits TLS versions prior to TLS 1.2 when using SNMP.

The text refers specifically to SNMPv3 and (D)TLS 1.3, but it may apply to future versions of these protocols and is backwards compatible with (D)TLS 1.2. Where it matters, it follows the SNMP terminology of RFC 3411. The terms "client" and "server" mean the two ends of the TLS connection: the client opens it and the server listens for it.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rules for locking up network-management messages were written for an older lock. This document says how to use the newer lock without breaking the old one.

sections.title: Fingerprints, Security Levels and Versions
sections.content:
Fingerprints. RFC 6353 defined the SnmpTLSFingerprint textual convention with a one-octet TLS 1.2 hash algorithm identifier. That identifier only applies to (D)TLS versions before 1.3, and the TLS community does not plan to add values to the "TLS HashAlgorithm" registry. RFC 9456 therefore says the identifier takes its values from a new IANA "SNMP-TLSTM HashAlgorithms" registry. Its initial values match the TLS registry but it can be extended without implying that new values may be used with TLS 1.2.

Security levels. RFC 3411 recognizes three levels: noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv and authPriv. Cipher suites for (D)TLS 1.3 from RFC 8446 provide both authentication and privacy, while those from RFC 9150 provide authentication only. Implementations MAY force (D)TLS 1.3 to allow only suites that provide both.

Versions. TLSTM MUST only be used with (D)TLS versions 1.2 and later.
sections.plainLanguage: Fingerprints are like ID numbers for certificates, and the list of ID formats is now kept in a new, extendable list. Also, only the newer locks may be used, and some of them only prove who you are without hiding the message.

sections.title: Additional Rules for TLS 1.3
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 implementations for SNMP MUST NOT enable the 0-RTT mode of session resumption, either sending or accepting, and MUST NOT automatically resend 0-RTT data if the server rejects it. The reason given is that no SNMP messages are "safe" if replayed: all incoming notifications or command responses are meant to be acted upon only once. RFC 8446 requires a profile naming safe messages for any application that wants 0-RTT, and within SNMP there are none.

Renegotiation is not supported, because TLS 1.3 does not support it. If a future TLS version supports it, this RFC should be updated to say what additional requirements apply.

Section 9 of RFC 8446 makes certain cipher suites, extensions and protocol invariants mandatory to implement when there is no application profile. This document does not specify a profile, so all those compliance requirements apply.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS 1.3 has a shortcut for reconnecting fast, but a thief could replay the same message. Since a network command must only run once, the shortcut is banned.

sections.title: The Updated SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB
sections.content:
Section 4 republishes the whole SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB module with revision 202311080000Z. Its revision note lists five changes: the clarified SnmpTLSFingerprint definition, key words capitalized per BCP 14, 'may not' replaced by 'MUST NOT' in several places, a clarification in SnmpTLSAddress, and cosmetic grammar and whitespace fixes.

The module keeps its structure. snmpTlstmCertToTSNTable lets a server map a client certificate to a security name, trying rows in priority order by snmpTlstmCertToTSNID, where lower numbers mean higher priority. If no row matches, the connection MUST be closed. snmpTlstmParamsTable holds the fingerprint of the client certificate to use, and snmpTlstmAddrTable lets a client verify the server by fingerprint or by host name. The module also defines session counters and two notifications about server certificate problems.
sections.plainLanguage: The module is a checklist the device keeps: which certificates it trusts, which name each one maps to, and counters for how many connections worked or failed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The threats and mitigations are covered throughout the document and in RFC 6353. TLS security considerations are in Section 10 and Appendix E of RFC 8446, and those for DTLS are in Section 11 of RFC 9147. Implementations should consider the latest recommendations in RFC 9325.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. It is RECOMMENDED that only SNMPv3 messages using the Transport Security Model (TSM) or another secure-transport-aware security model be sent over the TLSTM transport.
sections.plainLanguage: A good lock does not help if anyone inside the building can still open every drawer, so only the newer SNMP with proper access rules should use it.

sections.title: The SNMP-TLSTM HashAlgorithms Registry
sections.content:
IANA created the "SNMP-TLSTM HashAlgorithms" registry, with fields Value, Description, Recommended and References and a range of zero to 255. Initial values are: 0 none, 1 md5 and 2 sha1 (all marked N), 3 sha224, 4 sha256, 5 sha384 and 6 sha512 (marked Y), 7 Reserved, 8 Intrinsic (N), 9-223 Unassigned, and 224-255 Reserved for Private Use. Values 0 through 2 MUST NOT be used by implementations of this document and are listed for historical consistency.

The policy for updates is Expert Review, and designated experts are asked to consult the TLS registry review list. Any future additions to the "TLS HashAlgorithm" registry MUST be consistent with this registry's values.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a numbered list of ways to make a certificate's ID number. New ways can be added after experts check them, and a few old, weak ways are marked 'do not use'.

items.label: none
items.desc: Not recommended; MUST NOT be used.

items.desc: Not recommended; MUST NOT be used.
